## Automation: the silent enemy that has already won the game

The first electric motor to replace a human arm in Almuñécar was installed without ceremony or exceptional witnesses. It was in the mid-1980s, when a technician from a company in Granada climbed the bell tower of the Encarnación with a toolbox and came down leaving behind a mechanism capable of striking the bell with chronometric regularity. The bell ringers of the time watched him with a mixture of curiosity and suspicion, aware that this gadget did not need to learn the ringing patterns or inherit the memory of their elders. All it took was flipping a switch for the bronze to sound exactly as it always had, without nuances, without errors, and without the intervention of a human hand.

Automation arrived in Almuñécar with the promise of solving a practical problem: the lack of generational renewal. The parishes argued that an electric system was cheaper than keeping a person available at any hour of the day or night, and more reliable than depending on the health or willingness of an elderly man. The parish priests of the time saw in those devices an impeccable administrative solution, a way to ensure that the bells kept ringing even if there was no one left willing to climb the bell tower steps. What they failed to calculate was the symbolic cost of that decision, the silent loss of a language that could only be articulated with the hands.

Today, most of the local churches operate with electric systems that reproduce pre-recorded ringing patterns. The sound comes from a speaker or a mechanical hammer operated by a digital programmer, and it sounds identical at every funeral, every wedding, and every patron saint festival. The difference is imperceptible to the untrained ear, but the bell ringers who still remain in the municipality detect it instantly: the human pulse is missing, that minimal variation in rhythm that distinguished one bell ringer's toll from another's. The capacity to improvise is also gone, to extend a peal when the occasion warranted it or to shorten it when the wind threatened to destabilize the bell.

Local bell ringers admit that automation won the game decades ago. They say it with the resignation of someone who has watched their craft fade away without fanfare, without an exact moment to mark on the calendar as the day of defeat. The transition was gradual: first the daily mass rings were automated, then the funeral tolls, and finally the festive ones, until the bell ringer was relegated to a token role that is only claimed on rare occasions. Technology did not need to impose itself by force; it was enough to offer a more convenient and cheaper alternative for the parishes to adopt it without resistance.

The phrase that summarizes the position of the resisters belongs to Villavante, a bell ringer and scholar of manual ringing, who maintains that "AI will never be able to perform manual ringing." His statement is not a technophobic bravado, but a technical observation: manual ringing depends on the strength, balance, and sensitivity of a human body in relation to a specific bell, with its specific weight, its tilt, and even the temperature of the metal. An automatic system can reproduce a sequence of strikes, but it cannot feel the bell, it cannot adjust the gesture to the conditions of the moment, nor can it dialogue with the bronze as an experienced bell ringer does.

The paradox is that automation, presented as a guarantee of continuity, has accelerated the disappearance of the knowledge it sought to preserve. By no longer requiring the physical presence of the bell ringer, the chain of oral transmission that had kept the craft alive for centuries was interrupted. Young people no longer climb the bell tower because there is no one left to teach them, and there is no one to teach them because the parishes no longer needed apprentices. The result is a generational void that no electronic device can fill, a rupture in collective memory that manifests itself in the uniformity of today's ringing.

Automatic systems offer an advantage that manual bell ringers could never match: absolute punctuality. A digital programmer does not run late, does not get sick, and does not forget a funeral toll at three in the morning. The parishes value this reliability above any heritage considerations, and the parishioners have grown accustomed to a predictable sound that no longer demands interpretation. Manual ringing, with its variations and its silences laden with meaning, has become a hazy memory that only the oldest can clearly identify.

In Almuñécar, automation did not encounter organized opposition. The bell ringers of the 1980s were older men, accustomed to a craft that was already considered residual at the time, and they lacked the capacity to articulate a collective defense of their way of working. They accepted the new systems with the same naturalness with which they had accepted other transformations of the urban landscape, perhaps because they sensed that the battle was lost from the start. Technology arrived wrapped in the language of progress and modernization, and opposing it was tantamount to declaring oneself an enemy of the future.

The result is an impoverished soundscape, where all the bells sound the same and no ringing reveals the identity of the person executing it. The bell ringers who still climb the bell towers of Almuñécar do so out of personal conviction, not because the parishes require their services. Their presence is almost an act of silent resistance, a way of remembering that manual ringing was for centuries the sonic heartbeat of the community. Automation won the game, but it has not managed to completely erase the memory of what was lost.
